whoIsThisFor.heading: Who is the Advanced Field Service Accredited Professional exam for?

personas.label: Field Service leads
personas.description: You run Field Service for a company with many technicians and want to show you can set up scheduling and optimisation well.

personas.label: Consultants and admins
personas.description: You already hold the Agentforce Field Service Consultant credential or have built Field Service, and want to prove deeper skills.

personas.label: Career builders
personas.description: You specialise in Field Service projects and want a credential beyond the consultant exam.

examDifficulty.heading: Is the Advanced Field Service Accredited Professional Exam Hard?
examDifficulty.summary: It goes deeper than the Agentforce Field Service Consultant exam. Most questions are about scheduling: how policies, work rules and objectives shape the schedule, and which optimisation option fits a situation.
bullets: About 65% to pass, roughly 39 correct answers. Check the official guide for the current figure.
Scheduling depth. Scheduling policies, work rules, service objectives and the types of optimisation.
Real setups. Crews, multi-day work, shifts, inventory and the mobile app all come up.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: People who have tuned scheduling in a live Field Service org do best. Before you book. Aim for 75% or more on practice tests and make sure you can explain why a given appointment was or wasn't scheduled.

examFormat.heading: Advanced Field Service Accredited Professional Exam Format Explained
examFormat.intro: Accredited Professional exams are taken online. Here is what to expect:
examFormat.scenarioPercent: Most questions describe a scheduling or field problem, such as too much travel time or jobs needing two technicians, and ask what to change.
bestWayToPass: Know scheduling policies inside out: Work rules filter out technicians. Service objectives rank the ones that are left.
Learn the optimisation types: Global, in-day and resource schedule optimisation, and when to run each.
Understand crews and multi-day work: How jobs needing several people or several days are scheduled.
Know the mobile app: Offline use, data priming and what technicians can do in the field.

certificationCard.description: This exam tests advanced Field Service setup: scheduling policies and optimisation, complex appointments, crews, inventory, maintenance plans and the mobile app.

keyConcepts.h2: Advanced Field Service AP: Key Concepts for the Exam

blocks.heading: Scheduling & Optimization Engine
blocks.body: A **scheduling policy** tells the system how to choose a technician. **Work rules** are hard filters: the technician must have the right skills, work in the right territory and be available. **Service objectives** are soft goals that rank the remaining options, such as least travel, earliest arrival or preferred technician. You can weight objectives to show what matters most. **Optimisation** reruns scheduling across many appointments to improve the whole plan. **Global optimisation** usually runs overnight for the coming days. **In-day optimisation** fixes today's schedule after changes. **Resource schedule optimisation** improves one technician's day.

blocks.heading: Work Orders, Work Types & Service Appointments
blocks.body: A **work order** describes the job. A **work type** is a template that sets duration, required skills and whether a service appointment is created automatically. The **service appointment** is what gets scheduled on the calendar. Complex jobs can need **dependencies** between appointments, such as job B must start after job A ends. Long jobs can be scheduled as **multi-day work**. Jobs needing several people can use **service crews**, or several resources assigned to one appointment.

blocks.heading: Asset Management & Maintenance Plans
blocks.body: **Assets** are the products installed at a customer's site. **Maintenance plans** create work orders on a schedule, for example a check every six months, for one or many assets. You can set how far ahead work orders are generated and whether they are grouped. Asset history shows every visit and part used, which helps spot repeat failures. Warranty terms and entitlements can show what service the customer is owed.

blocks.heading: Inventory & Parts Management
blocks.body: **Locations** include warehouses and technicians' vans. **Product items** record how much of each part is at a location. Technicians use **product requests** to ask for parts, and **product transfers** move parts between locations. When a part is used on a job, it is logged as **product consumed**, which lowers stock. Required parts can be set on a work type, so the scheduler can favour technicians who already carry them.

blocks.heading: Mobile Worker Experience & Offline
blocks.body: The **Field Service mobile app** lets technicians see their schedule, update work orders, capture signatures and log parts and time. It works **offline**: data is downloaded (primed) to the device ahead of time, and changes sync when the connection returns. Admins choose what data is primed so the app stays fast. Mobile flows and app extensions add custom steps, such as safety checklists. Technicians can also update their status, which keeps the dispatcher console accurate.

scenarioTips.h2: How to Pass the Salesforce Advanced Field Service Accredited Professional Exam
scenarioTips.intro: Most questions are about why the schedule looks the way it does, or how to set up a tricky job. Separate the hard rules from the soft goals.

blocks.heading: Optimization Engine Architecture
blocks.body: Global optimisation for the next few days, usually overnight. In-day optimisation to repair today. Resource schedule optimisation for one person's day.

blocks.heading: Complex Scheduling Scenarios
blocks.body: Jobs in a fixed order use dependencies. Long jobs use multi-day work. Jobs needing several people use crews or multiple resources.

blocks.heading: Resource Capacity Planning
blocks.body: Capacity-based resources, such as contractors, are scheduled by hours or jobs per period, not by exact slots.

blocks.heading: Field Service Analytics
blocks.body: Track first-time fix rate, travel time, utilisation and on-time arrival to see where scheduling can improve.

blocks.heading: Mobile App Advanced Configuration
blocks.body: Control offline priming, add mobile flows for checklists, and keep technician status updated for dispatchers.

nextCertsAfter.heading: Next Certifications After This AP
nextCertsAfter.intro: Good next steps after Advanced Field Service:

sampleQuestions.question: A technician without the right certification keeps being suggested for electrical jobs. What should be changed?
options: Increase the job's duration
Add a service objective covering the preferred technician for the account
A required skill on the work type, plus a skill work rule
Turn off optimisation
sampleQuestions.explanation: Work rules are hard filters. A skill work rule removes technicians who don't have the required skill.
whyWrong: Duration doesn't affect skills.
Objectives only rank candidates. They can't rule someone out.
Turning off optimisation doesn't stop wrong suggestions.

sampleQuestions.question: The business wants schedules that cut down on driving time; while still meeting all the rules. What should be adjusted?
options: The minimise travel objective weight
The number of work types
The page layout
The serial numbers held on the assets
sampleQuestions.explanation: Service objectives rank options. Giving more weight to minimise travel makes the scheduler prefer shorter trips.
whyWrong: Work type count doesn't shape travel.
Layouts don't affect scheduling.
Serial numbers have no effect on travel.

sampleQuestions.question: Several technicians called in sick this morning and today's schedule is now full of gaps and conflicts. Which optimisation fits?
options: Resource schedule optimisation for one technician
No optimisation, just wait
Global optimisation for the next two weeks
In-day optimisation
sampleQuestions.explanation: In-day optimisation is meant to repair today's schedule after changes like absences or emergencies.
whyWrong: Fixing one technician doesn't solve the wider problem.
Waiting leaves customers without visits.
Global optimisation looks further ahead and usually runs overnight.

sampleQuestions.question: A job needs two technicians to work together at the same time. What is a good way to schedule it?
options: Make the job twice as long
Create one appointment and hope two people turn up
A service crew, or several resources on it
Schedule it twice on different days
sampleQuestions.explanation: Crews and multiple-resource scheduling let one appointment be served by more than one person at once.
whyWrong: A longer job is still one person.
Hoping doesn't schedule anyone.
Two different days means they aren't working together.

sampleQuestions.question: Installing a pump must finish before the electrical connection job can start. How should this be set up?
options: A note in the description
One very long appointment
A dependency on the appointments
Two unrelated appointments
sampleQuestions.explanation: Appointment dependencies tell the scheduler that one job must finish before the other starts.
whyWrong: A note doesn't affect scheduling.
One long job can't use two different skill sets well.
Unrelated appointments might be scheduled in the wrong order.

sampleQuestions.question: A building's lifts must be inspected every 3 months. How should the work orders be created?
options: Creating each of them by hand every quarter
A maintenance plan for the lift assets
A report emailed to the team
A Case for each inspection
sampleQuestions.explanation: Maintenance plans create work orders on a schedule for the assets they cover.
whyWrong: Manual creation is easy to forget.
A report doesn't create the work.
Cases are for issues; and still need manual creation.

sampleQuestions.question: A technician uses a spare part on a job. How should this be recorded so stock stays correct?
options: Log it as a product consumed on the work order
Delete the product item
Add the part to the work type's required products
Create a product request
sampleQuestions.explanation: Product consumed records the part used and reduces the stock at the technician's location.
whyWrong: Deleting the product item removes all stock records.
Required products describe what a job needs, they don't record usage.
A product request asks for more stock, it doesn't record what was used.

sampleQuestions.question: A technician's van is low on a part. How should they ask for more?
options: Add the part as a required product on the work type
Log a product consumed with a negative amount
Create a product transfer back to the warehouse
Create a product request
sampleQuestions.explanation: Product requests are how technicians ask for parts to be sent to their location.
whyWrong: Required products describe what a job needs, they don't order stock.
Product consumed records parts used, not parts needed.
A transfer moves parts that are already approved. The request comes first.

sampleQuestions.question: Technicians often work in basements with no signal. What must be set up so the mobile app still works?
options: Offline data priming for the records they need
Moving the jobs to a different service territory
A mobile flow that saves data to a custom object
Shorter appointment durations
sampleQuestions.explanation: The app downloads needed records ahead of time and syncs changes once the connection is back.
whyWrong: Territory changes don't give the device any data offline.
A flow still needs data on the device, and the data must be primed first.
Duration has nothing to do with connectivity.

sampleQuestions.question: Technicians must complete a safety checklist before starting each job in the mobile app. What should be added?
options: A dashboard
A new scheduling policy
A mobile flow on the work order
A newly created service territory
sampleQuestions.explanation: Mobile flows add guided steps, like checklists, inside the mobile app.
whyWrong: Dashboards show data, not steps.
Scheduling policies choose technicians, not job steps.
Territories group areas, not tasks.

sampleQuestions.question: A contractor company should get up to 40 hours of work per week, without exact time slots. How should they be set up?
options: As a location
As a capacity-based resource
As a regular resource with a fixed shift
As an asset
sampleQuestions.explanation: Capacity-based resources are scheduled by hours or job count per period, which fits contractors.
whyWrong: Locations are places, not people.
Regular resources are scheduled into exact slots.
Assets are equipment at customer sites.

sampleQuestions.question: A scheduling policy has work rules and service objectives. What is the difference?
options: Objectives remove the candidates and then the work rules rank them
Work rules exclude; objectives rank what is left
Both only apply to mobile users
They are the same thing
sampleQuestions.explanation: Rules are pass or fail filters. Objectives score the remaining options.
whyWrong: That has them the wrong way round.
Both apply to all scheduling.
They do different jobs in the policy.

sampleQuestions.question: Customers keep booking slots that technicians can't reach in time. What should be checked?
options: Travel time settings, such as street-level routing
The work order priority field
The appointment booking slot length only
The scheduling policy's preferred resource objective
sampleQuestions.explanation: Accurate travel time depends on routing settings and territories. Poor estimates lead to impossible slots.
whyWrong: Priority changes order, not travel time.
Slot length doesn't fix wrong travel estimates.
Preferring a technician doesn't make travel times accurate.

sampleQuestions.question: A new hire should only get simple jobs for their first month. How can this be done?
options: Give them no territory
Basic skills at the right levels
Turn off their user account
Put them in a separate org
sampleQuestions.explanation: Skills and skill levels let the scheduler match only suitable jobs to each person.
whyWrong: No territory means no jobs at all.
A turned-off user can't work at all.
A separate org cuts them off from the rest.

sampleQuestions.question: A manager wants to know how often technicians fix the problem on the first visit. Which measure fits?
options: Average travel time
On-time arrival rate
Resource utilisation
First-time fix rate
sampleQuestions.explanation: First-time fix rate shows how often jobs are finished without a return visit, which is key for service quality.
whyWrong: Travel time measures driving, not fix quality.
On-time arrival measures punctuality, not whether a return visit was needed.
Utilisation shows how busy technicians are, not whether jobs were fixed first time.
